items.definition: The tendency to forget information that is easy to find online, while remembering how to find it.
The habit of holding your own beliefs with the right amount of confidence: strong when the evidence is strong, weak when it is weak.
The skill of finding, judging and using information: telling a primary source from an opinion, and evidence from an anecdote.
The state in which incoming information exceeds the capacity to process it, so each new item reduces the value of the ones before it.
The total amount of mental effort being used by working memory at one time.
The market in which businesses compete for people's limited attention and resell it to advertisers.
The proportion of useful information (signal) to everything else (noise) in a stream of content.
Familiarity with the surface of many topics without understanding of how any of them works.
Reading bad news repeatedly on purpose, because the subject holds your attention. A specific habit, not a synonym for scrolling.
items.example: That was an hour of doomscrolling, and I felt worse each time I checked.

items.definition: Someone who earns income that does not depend on one country and who lives in several places over a year.
items.example: As a digital nomad, I move when the client contract ends.

items.definition: A residence permit for people who work remotely for foreign employers or clients without a local work permit.
items.example: The nomad visa requires proof of income above a monthly threshold.

items.definition: The status that decides which country has a claim to tax your income, usually based on where you spend most of your time.
items.example: Tax residency is the part nobody checks before they book the flight.

items.definition: A building where residents rent a room and share a kitchen and common areas, and where nomads often find a community.
items.example: I took a room in a coliving for a month and made friends in a week.

items.definition: A paid workspace where people work in the same room, usually by the day or the month, with a desk and reliable internet.
items.example: A co-working space costs less than the coffee I would buy sitting in a café all day.

items.definition: Staying in one place for weeks or months instead of moving on every few days, which is what makes long-term work possible.
items.example: Slow travel costs less and lets you actually know the place.

items.definition: Working from a shared space other than your own home, which many employers offer or pay for.
items.example: My company gave me an offsiting budget of two hundred dollars a month.

items.definition: The disorientation you feel when the everyday rules of a place stop matching the ones you grew up with.
items.example: Culture shock hit me the week I could not find a supermarket open after six.

items.definition: Judging another culture by the standards of your own, and reading every difference as a mistake.
items.example: Calling a local custom rude is ethnocentrism, not an observation.

items.definition: A rule everybody follows without discussing it, such as removing shoes before entering a home.
items.example: The norm here is to arrive ten minutes late, and everyone reads the time differently.

items.definition: A line that is not crossed at all, such as asking about somebody's salary.
items.example: Asking about his pay was a taboo, so I did not ask.

items.definition: Short, friendly conversation with someone you do not know well. Its purpose is contact, not important information.
items.example: We had some small talk about the rain and ended up talking for an hour.

items.definition: The finished state of living comfortably in a new culture, when the local way no longer feels strange.
items.example: After a year, adaptation: I queue without thinking about it now.

items.definition: The ABS has a fault. Normal braking still works, but the wheels can lock under heavy braking. Severity level 3 — Warning. Action: Have the ABS checked. Until then, brake earlier and more gently..
The distance the car travels from the moment the driver touches the brake to the moment the car stops.
items.example: On a wet road the braking distance is longer than on a dry road.

items.definition: The grip between the tyre and the road, and it is what turns the car's speed into a stop.
items.example: There is little traction on ice, so the car slides even at a low speed.

items.definition: The moment when a wheel stops turning while the car is still moving.
items.example: The front wheel went into lock-up and the steering went light.

items.definition: Braking at the limit of grip by pressing and releasing the pedal before the wheel locks.
items.example: Without ABS the driver has to use threshold braking.

items.definition: The loss of braking power when the brakes are hot, so that the pedal goes soft.
items.example: After the long descent the brakes faded and the pedal felt weak.

items.definition: A small part at each wheel that reports how fast that wheel is turning.
items.example: A damaged sensor at one wheel can switch the ABS off.

items.definition: The part of the brake that changes the brake pressure at a wheel when the system asks it to.
items.example: The modulator holds the pressure at the wheel that is about to lock.

items.definition: The material under the tyre: tarmac, concrete, gravel, sand, mud, snow, ice or leaves.
items.example: The road surface was loose gravel, so a locked wheel was the shorter stop.

items.definition: Applying the brake with steadily increasing pressure instead of one sudden push.
items.example: In heavy traffic she used progressive braking and the stop was smooth.

items.definition: Slowing the car with the engine and the gearbox instead of with the brake pedal.
items.example: On the long descent he used engine braking and the brakes stayed cool.

items.definition: The time between seeing a hazard and moving the brake pedal.
items.example: The reaction time of the driver is part of the distance the car travels before the brakes work.

items.definition: The lever beside the driver's seat that holds the car still; it is also called the parking brake.
items.example: She pulled the handbrake to lock the rear wheels on the ice.

items.definition: Coarse salt that softens the water in a dishwasher so that detergent can work. It goes in the round cap at the bottom of the tub.
items.example: The salt symbol has come on, so I am filling the salt cap.

items.definition: The powder or tablet that does the cleaning. It goes in the main compartment of the drawer, marked with two vertical bars.
items.example: Put one tablet in the compartment with the two bars.

items.definition: A liquid added to the wide compartment of the drawer that makes water sheet off the dishes so they dry without spots.
items.example: The rinse aid symbol is lit, so I need to top up the wide compartment.

items.definition: The last stage of a wash, in which the drum turns fast to push water out of the fabric.
items.example: A higher spin speed means the washing comes out drier.

items.definition: The car is in an economy mode: it saves fuel, and often responds more gently. Severity level 1 — Information / Status. Action: Nothing to do..
